newsitem.title: USA: Vermont moves to deregulate electric utilities.
newsitem.headline: Vermont moves to deregulate electric utilities.

text.p: Vermont took a step toward deregulating its electric utility industry, with a goal of introducing competition to the state's power companies by January 1998.

A 141-page report issued by the Vermont Public Service Board, the state's utility regulatory agency, contains nine recommendations to end the utilities'geographic monopolies without driving the companies out of business or hurting electric customers.

But the Burlington Electric Department, Vermont's largest city-owned utility, says deregulation could leave the city liable for the department's $90 million debt, most of it associated with the city's ten-year old 50-megawatt wood burning power plant.

"We're concerned that we'll lose our largest commercial customers to competing utilities," says Steve Burroughs, Burlington Electric's general manager. Mayor Peter Clavelle has urged Vermont regulators "to be conservative" and slow down the rush to deregulate.

Public Service Board chairman Richard Cowart says deregulation could shave 10 percent or more off Vermont electric bills. But chief executives at the state's two dominant power companies, CVPS and Green Mountain Power corp, say the savings could drive them under if deregulation prohibits passing the so-called stranded cost onto ratepayers.

At a Burlington conference last month, officials with the two utilities estimated Vermont's total electric power debt at up to $1.4 billion - most of it tied up in expensive long-term contracts for power purchases from Hydro Quebec.
A final draft of the report will be submitted to the Vermont legislature in January.

Although the report warns that the companies will not be allowed to charge their ratepayers the total cost of prior power investments, reaction from Vermont's largest electric company, Central Vermont Public Service Corp, was positive.

"They have included consumer protection, environmental protection, (and) protecting utilities against bankruptcy," CVPS spokesman Steven Costello said. "They have addressed almost all of the issues very well on first blush."
